long.hook: Say you make metal parts, and before every batch you simulate a test ring being pressed, to predict how it will deform. You have two simulators. One is careful and trustworthy: thirty-four seconds a run. The other is quick and rough: two seconds, and always a little off. You get one hour of computer time. How do you spend it?
long.goal: Because what you really want isn't a pile of simulations. It's a model that answers for any ring, any friction, any material, in an instant, and tells you how far to trust that answer. Every simulation is one lesson for that model.
long.budget: An hour buys about a hundred careful lessons. Or eighteen hundred sloppy ones. Neither sounds right.
long.three_fine: Go careful only, and the model knows a hundred points perfectly, and nothing in between. Where it hasn't looked, it guesses. And sometimes it guesses straight through a feature it never saw.
long.three_cheap: Go cheap only, and something sneakier happens. The model learns the cheap simulator's answer beautifully, down to the last detail. But that answer is wrong, and the model has no way to know. It becomes confidently wrong.
long.three_mix: So do both. Let the cheap runs sketch the whole landscape. Then spend a few careful runs measuring how far off that sketch is. The model learns the shape from one, and the correction from the other.
long.results: We tried all of this on a real forming simulator, and scored every model on a hundred fresh test cases. The mix had the lowest error. And when it claimed to be ninety-five percent sure, it was right ninety-one percent of the time. Cheap runs alone? Right two times in three, while claiming the same confidence.
long.confirm: A good result on eight trials isn't proof. So we wrote the test down in advance, including exactly how we would judge it, and ran twelve more. The mix won eleven of them, with about thirty percent less error for the same hour.
long.picking: One last question. Who decides where the runs go? Here, mostly nobody: a Latin hypercube spreads them evenly before anything is run. We also tried handing that decision to the model, letting it choose the runs it was least sure about. The even spread is the one behind every number you've just seen.
long.takeaway: Same hour of compute. About thirty percent less error. And a model that knows what it doesn't know. The idea is simple, and surprisingly few teams use it.

short.s1: Two simulators of the same test. One slow and trustworthy, one fast and a little off. One hour of compute. How do you spend it?
short.s2: Careful runs only: the model guesses between too few points. Cheap only: it learns the wrong answer perfectly, and is sure of it. Mix them: cheap runs draw the shape, a few careful ones fix the offset.
short.s3: On a real forming simulator: thirty percent less error for the same hour, honest about its uncertainty, confirmed on twelve trials we committed to in advance.
short.s4: The runs were spread evenly in advance, a Latin hypercube. We also tried letting the model choose. The full story is on GitHub.
